title.en: Exploring geometric themes: fractals and visualising solids

text.en: Look at a fern: each leaf looks like a small copy of the whole fern, and each small leaf has even smaller copies.

A fractal is a self-similar shape: the same pattern repeats at smaller and smaller scales.
Ferns, trees and coastlines show this repeating pattern in nature.
The Sierpinski carpet starts with a square cut into 9 equal smaller squares and the central square removed.
The same step is repeated on each of the 8 remaining squares, and so on without end.
At step n the number of remaining squares is 8ⁿ, so it is 1, 8, 64, 512 and so on.
The number of holes grows too: each step adds 8ⁿ⁻¹ new holes, so holes in total are 1, 9, 73 and so on.
Solids can be visualised from different directions: top, front and side views show different faces.
A net is a flat pattern that folds into a solid, so a cube has a net made of 6 squares.
A cross-section is the face we get when we cut a solid with a plane, and the shape depends on the direction of the cut.
Practising with drawings and paper models helps us imagine a solid from its views.

problem.en: How many squares remain at step 3 of the Sierpinski carpet?

text.en: At each step every square is replaced by 8 smaller squares.

prompt.en: Why is the fern a fractal?

requiredIdeas.en: It is made of smaller copies of itself.
The copies repeat at smaller scales.

points.en: Fractals repeat the same pattern at smaller scales.
The Sierpinski carpet keeps 8 of 9 squares each step, giving 8ⁿ squares.
Nets, views and cross-sections help us visualise solids.
